opening: Near-expiry stock, routed by AI agents. One yes from a person.

lines.text: Every day, across India, good products run out of time before they run out of demand.
A batch waits in a distributor's godown as its best-before date draws closer.
Once it crosses the quick-commerce gates, the modern-trade shelves close to it.
What usually follows is a write-off: the stock destroyed, the GST credit reversed, and perfectly good food in a landfill.
The brand loses, the distributor loses, and the people who would have bought it never get the chance.
Smart-Clearance changes that.
It is a software-as-a-service platform for manufacturers, built around an ecosystem of AI agents.
Every brand gets its own workspace, set up for its supply chain: its distributors and super stockists, its quick-commerce gates, its exits and its rules.
Inside it, ten agents work together along nine stops.
They detect, verify, value, decide, execute, settle and report.
And at the one moment that matters, a person says yes. Nothing moves before that.
A platform of its own kind: the whole chain on one system, from the manufacturer to the distributor, the kirana, the buyer and the food bank, each acting in their own name.
It starts with the stock data the distributor already has.
The Data agent maps the stock export field by field, so nothing is keyed in twice.
Every morning, the Watcher checks every batch at every distributor against its sell-through and the quick-commerce gates.
When a batch will not sell in time, the supply planner is told on her phone, in plain words, with the write-off it would mean.
The batch gets a page of its own: where it stands, and what comes next.
Before anything is priced, the batch is verified.
Vision asks the distributor for one photo of the carton label.
It reads the batch number, the dates and the MRP, checks the barcode and the FSSAI licence, and matches them to the stock record.
One photo from a phone, and the batch is real.
Now the Valuer prices every exit: the kirana cluster, the marketplace, the staff sale, the food bank, and the quick-commerce channels the batch can still reach.
Each one is priced per unit, after costs and GST, against what destroying the stock would cost.
The Router then splits the batch across the exits, and explains its reasoning in plain language.
The plan lands on the planner's desk with everything she needs to decide.
She approves it once. The approval is logged, with who, when, and the device.
The distributor is told the plan in his own language, with a pause button, and the agents set off.
Outreach sends the kirana cluster its scheme, in Hindi, straight to each shop's phone.
A shop sees the offer and its margin, and orders in a tap. Each order gets its own tax invoice, in the distributor's name.
The Lister puts the rest on the near-expiry marketplace, hidden from the brand's own territories.
When a buyer bids, the Negotiator answers in the distributor's name, holds the reserve, and closes the deal. The buyer pays the token; the truck is loaded.
At the godown, the staff sale opens, recorded on one consolidated UPI receipt that Vision reads and reconciles.
Packs with enough shelf life go to a food bank, as sealed cartons: the pickup booked, the FSSAI checklist drafted, and the food bank's own receipt issued.
And the van round delivers the scheme to every shop that ordered.
This is where most clearances fall apart: the paperwork. Here, it is automatic.

The Paperwork agent drafts the whole pack: the distributor's tax invoice, ready to issue from Tally with its e-invoice; the brand's credit note, so the distributor ends whole; the GST memo, with the input credit kept and reversed under section 17(5)(h); the FSSAI checklist; and an invoice to every kirana.
Every paper is laid out as a signed PDF with the firm's stamp, and reviewed by the planner.
The distributor sees his own papers on his own portal, ready to download.

chapters.title: When it does not go as planned

lines.text: Sometimes it does not go as planned. Some shops do not order, and stock is still left at the godown on expiry day.
Smart-Clearance handles that too, fully automated.
The distributor is asked to destroy the expired packs through an authorised agency, with the evidence: a photo before, a photo after, and the agency's certificate.
Vision checks the photos against the batch and the count.
The certificate of destruction is signed in place, on the distributor's screen: the agency's officer, two independent witnesses, and the distributor.
The planner reviews the evidence and gives her second yes. The expiry credit note and the destruction certificate are issued, and the batch closes, its record complete.
When a batch closes, Impact posts the ledger.
Money: what was recovered against the write-off, batch by batch, quarter by quarter.
GST: the input credit kept and reversed, invoice by invoice, ready for the accountant.
Impact: the food kept out of landfill, the CO₂e avoided, the packs donated, and the BRSR line with its evidence.
And every batch keeps its record: the photos, the approvals, and the audit trail of every agent and person.
The brand recovers. The distributor ends whole. The kiranas earn. The food bank receives.
One platform. Ten agents. One yes.
